author: martincsweiss
text:
Co-author here - first paper from my postdoc accepted to NeurIPS main conference.

We built a way to sample diverse ideas in machine learning - ideas that make scientific sense, but that no existing research community is positioned to propose.

In short, the way it works is like this:

1. Take 16,068 LLM papers (NeurIPS, ICLR, ICML, ACL, EMNLP, 2017 to 2025) are broken into 273 "idea atoms". Every paper, and every candidate idea, becomes a set of atoms.

2. Train a Coherence Model: a 42.8M-parameter transformer trained on papers as sequences of atoms. Basically a language model whose tokens are ideas.

3. Train a Cognitive-Availability Model: a dual encoder trained on the publication histories of 39,791 researchers, which predicts where each person could plausibly go next.

4. Use those models to score sampled tuples using reciprocal rank fusion (you want ideas that go together well, but that are not cognitively available to anyone).

We tested it in a bunch of ways. One interesting one was that we took all the papers at the end of 2024, then checked which high-scoring tuples showed up in 2025 papers. It worked well - one examples is an ICLR 2025 oral, goes from rank 1,489 with coherence alone to the top 25 of 1.14M samples.

author: martincsweiss
text:
Great question - the "universe" of venues we address is centered on peer-reviewed machine learning like ICML, ICLR, NeurIPS, COLM because (a) we have expertise in this area and so can therefore judge the quality and (b) it's all open access.

Therefore, the further you get away from the topic of ML, the less dense our coverage. Frankly, it's a tough to editorial choice to determine which research directions and therefore which proposals to include. ML is quite multi-disciplinary. And people who have a few papers in ML but many in (e.g.) medicine get upset when their profile is sparse. But we can't possibly produce good proposals in medicine due to its tendency to be closed-access.

author: martincsweiss

I'd say science is somewhat fractal in this sense. A research area contains topics, those topics have sub-topics, those sub-topics have competing lines that "talk" to each other, etc. So if it works in core ML that means it's working for RL and deep learning and computer vision and NLP -- which is kind of cross-domain.

That said - we believe the method does need to have sufficient data to model the conceptual density. So it'll not work in closed-science areas.

You can think of it like Althea (our agent) being an area chair and moderating a discussion to determine how to update pages. author: martincsweiss
text:
Not at all a tangent. We run a backtest in section 5.2 with pre-2025 scores to recover 2025 directions.

We rank all 1.14M three-atom combinations and check them against the 2,424 that appeared in 2025 papers. Using coherence alone, the top 10k (under 1% of the space) recovers 31.4% of them, about 36x chance. Adding the availability score trades some of that for more genuinely new combinations, ones whose atoms had never appeared together before. Judge Decoding (ICLR 2025 oral) moves from rank ~1,489 to rank 1 of 1.14M.

To your point about diffusion, I agree that just having a good idea is not enough. Politics / institutional inertia is the primary determinant of policy.

There was an incredible amount of investment into high-speed programmable power looms, and there were a number of innovations (later rediscovered by computer architects) targeted at 'card-saving techniques' to reduce the labor required to card-punch the designs, and to reduce the down-time of the looms. 'Double Data Rate' card readers (with a design interleaved on two chains running at half frequency), SIMD-style one-reader/many-loom setups, 'cross-border' looms that switched between two separate card loops just like a 'branch' instruction, machines to copy chains of punch cards.

What you're saying might have been true in the 18th century or earlier, but things were highly mechanized by the 19th century, and there was a lot of motivation to keep the big expensive looms highly utilized and amortize investment in punch card sets across lots of production runs.

One of the proposal papers caught my eye:

 > " ... a ligand that binds tightly and stays bound a long time should produce a strong intracellular signal, a weak binder a faint one."

When a ligand binds to the ligand binding pocket, the contact points it makes with the proteins inside (called "cofactors") and the strength of each contact point (measured in van der Waals force) modulate the distinct transcriptional effect.

This is called "conformation": the shape it takes in the ligand binding pocket.

So it is not necessarily residence time and overall binding affinity that modulate transcriptional effect.

A very good example of this is the androgen Trestolone/MENT, which is an order of magnitude more potent than Testosterone but displays similar relative binding affinity for the androgen receptor:

 [LINK] 

This potency is due to the specific conformational shape it takes within the AR binding pocket.

The academic literature has a problem in that it is relatively incoherent. Each new paper provides some small advance, with only a meager indication of how it fits into the known science in the area, its importance, and its consistency with previous results. It also remains in the corpus if later publications disprove its results or fail to replicate them. Only slowly do the aggregate of published results find their way into more systematic and complete authoritative texts.

AI promises to solve this problem by absorbing the entire corpus quickly and making a coherent whole available for further research and progress. It will be particularly useful if it can immediately flag any conflicts and inconsistencies, as well as any new relationships with other results not indicated in citations.

author: adrianmonk
text:
I skimmed the paper, and it seems to be saying something different.

Basically, there are often different ways of putting a particular idea into words. Sometimes the longer way might be clearer, and the shorter way might be more confusing. If you care about being understood, sometimes you will use the wordy option. This is what humans usually do.

However, LLMs have context windows. All else being equal, verbosity eats up more context. If the LLM is trained (with reinforcement learning) to reason most effectively, it can do that by using terse phrasing. Especially on certain tasks that really need a large context window. Why? Because being terse is like getting a larger context window for free.

But in another sense, it's not really free. You're trading off clarity for context window. Sometimes you have to choose between verbose+clear and terse+unclear. If you're biased toward terse, that will also shift you toward unclear.

I do agree that LLMs are verbose sometimes, though. I think they are also trained to please the user, and they see sharing extra knowledge and insights as a way to do that. I don't think this idea is in conflict with what the paper says. If an LLM's training rewards both spitting out neat bonus info and doing reasoning that requires making the most of its limited context window, then that LLM may generate a large quantity of text which is written in a slightly terse and confusing style.

text:
Pacing is extremely important in writing. The way one speaks out loud is often not the way that they actually read in their head. Speaking out loud has three parts to it in conception, translation, and vocation. Conception as to what the thought is, translation of that thought to language, and vocation of the language through visuals or sound. Reading only shares the translation portion, but also has organization added to it where you need to organize the information as you ingest it. As such, it's important to format whatever you're writing so that it can be organized first and translated second. People look at the words linearly but don't ingest the information linearly. This is a principle many literary jokes are built upon.

ChatGPT, Gemini, and whatever else do not in fact have the capability to understand that interaction between organization and translation. They process the information linearly, organize it linearly, and translate it linearly. That's what makes it so strange to read. A must lead to B which must lead to C. A cannot connect to C and then circle back to B which is connected to both A and C obliquely. It's a failure in understanding language and how it is used.

I think I might be slightly opposite of you, but not very far opposite. I prefer reading a precise and accurate sentence that - when understood - clearly describes the intent without a shred of doubt much more than an easy to understand sentence that I find ambiguous because, to understand it, it requires context and a social agreement that nobody is trying to trick people.

I had a friend once that kept using open-ended phrasings and ambiguous descriptions because (I think) he enjoyed the feeling of power or control that the confusion and miscommunication introduced. Like if he were to "run to the stores" you could ask what he was buying and he'd follow up with a "oh, I didn't say I was buying anything, I'm just going for a run". If I have to guess which of the variations of meanings is the intended one, then the communication has failed in my book, regardless of how easy it was to understand the sentence.

author: Sharlin

In British English it’s entirely standard (and common) for grammatically singular collective nouns to take a plural verb and be referred to with a plural pronoun:

"The ManU have won three out of their last four matches."

"The Parliament have had heated debates over the NIH budget."

"Tesla introduced their newest EV model last week."

Any competent English teacher should know this.

Also, there’s no "correct" language outside of how it’s actually used. Linguists are the first to explain that their job is to describe, not to prescribe.

"When to use a singular verb

When to use a plural verb

When the members of a collective noun are performing an action as individuals, use a plural verb. In this case, all or some members of the group are doing something independently of the other members; the group is not acting together as a unit.

LLM reinforcement learning improves those tasks by having the agents "reason" until they hit a verifiable output state that passes a black or white test. So they learn language which is tuned to the task in a silo, never communicating with anyone or anything.

In contrast, most human communication and writing is intended for other humans, and we constantly hit failures here that we learn to iterate on and improve. Humans who do math do so with the constraints that their math needs to be reviewed by another human and in the context that all their writing needs to be understood by another human.

The process causes a warped and compressed version of language.

One construction I'm surprised the paper doesn't mention (although, to be fair, I'm sure they had plenty of options to choose from... and you have to draw the line somewhere :P) is that LLMs love to use transitive verbs intransitively[0], in a way I almost never see in human writing. At best it makes sentences weirdly ambiguous, at worst it makes them borderline incomprehensible, and it's especially annoying in technical contexts where precise language should be non-negotiable. Like, yes, I can make an educated guess about what it's trying to say, but if your so-called documentation requires readers/users to make educated guesses then something has gone terribly wrong.

[0] An example would be something like:

"The user presses a button, and the form submits."

There are valid intransitive uses of "submit," but none that make sense in this context. In this case "submit" either requires an object (like "the form submits data"--plus maybe an indirect object, like "the form submits data to the server") or should be swapped for "the form is submitted" if you absolutely don't want to supply an object.

author: teraflop
text:
I sort of agree but I think the issue is more subtle.

Languages change over time, and one of the well-documented "laws" of language change (using that term very fuzzily) is that people like to take irregular features of a language and generalize them to make them more regular. And there are many English verbs (particularly verbs expressing a change of state) which can be used transitively or intransitively, with equal validity:

> "I opened the door" -- "the door was opened" -- "the door opened"

> "the heat melted the ice" -- "the ice was melted" -- "the ice melted"

> "the impact cracked the glass" -- "the glass was cracked" -- "the glass cracked"

This generalization has been common, especially in jargon-y contexts, long before the rise of LLMs. A pedant might insist on saying "wait for the compiler to compile the code", and Merriam-Webster thinks "compile" can only be used transitively. But I think most developers would say "wait for the code to compile [i.e. be compiled]" is fine too. (see e.g. this XKCD comic from 2007: [LINK] )

In my view, this usage is completely fine as an occasional thing, especially when the social process of language change has normalized it over time for a particular verb. The issue is that LLMs drastically overuse it and pepper it everywhere. Just like "it's not X, it's Y", which is fine occasionally in human writing, but has become a dreadful cliche through overuse.

For AI, the borders seem to have blurred a bit between academic scientists (e.g. at universities) and external scientists at companies or even private people). author: dannyw
text:
Pretty much. See “Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models”, a must read IMO [LINK] 

Compute, data, and parameter count are the three logarithmic values that correspond to model performance.

So if you find ways of improving training efficiency (the simplest conceptually is probably local/global sliding window attention like Gemma; the latest DeepSeek and Kimis have quite fancy ones), you will be able to have more effective compute, and train smarter models while keeping data and param count the same.

If you find this fascinating and want to dive more, I encourage checking out nanochat (solid GPT-2 repro; minimal LoC); and trying to make architectural tweaks with a coding agent.

“Learning through experimentation” has never been easier or more fun in my opinion. If you have a GPU, even an older 8GB card (or a few bucks for Runpod), you can pretrain your own small language model and start experimenting / tweaking it.

It would not be the discrete qubit form we are trying to do, which is impossible in a noisy wet environment, but something analog and stochastic.

Both are possible.

Also note that our current chips, in spite of the tiny feature sizes and a ton of optimization work, are not even close to the lower limit for energy cost of computation. They still are not very efficient.

text:
I agree with the framing but the claim is too strong.

I don't think Grassmannian manifolds are necessarily a better representation than simple query/key inner products. It's a valid solution, and it does have advantages in some cases.

The Grassmannian is only preserving the subspace orientation, so we lose information about the actual linear map and basically throw out its basis.

Like everything, this is a trade off. You're trading information for a lower rank representation.

I'm still reading through the paper on the implementation side, but the other caveat I'd be wary of is compute. Does this projection add MACs to the overall model which would make inference slightly slower even with lower rank representations? I don't know. Like with any technique that trades constrained information representation for space/compute you _are_ widening your search space during training. I'd be curious what the impact of this is on relative data needed to train a model using this architecture versus "regular" attention.

author: ErroneousBosh
text:
> most cases have giant holes in the side (case windows) acting as slot antennas.

They won't act as slot antennas unless they are tuned to the frequency you wish to transmit on, and actually electrically connected on each side to your transmitter.

author: superkuh
text:
Correct. But also, an antenna doesn't have to be exactly resonant at the desired frequency in order to help. You can see this most often in the antennas people use for HF, which to be resonant have to be giant and many meters in size, but instead they use small non-resonant antenna that still transmit enough, even at very low efficiency, to radiate an annoying amount of interference.

Not having a giant slot antenna is a lot better than having a slot antenna. Even if the slot antenna is best resonant at mid-VHF (ie, ~144 MHz which is what many GPU RAMs are blasting at at high current).

And just as important: a huge hole is a hole. Even if it's not acting as an efficient antenna. It's basically an entire side of the case missing.

author: ErroneousBosh
text:
Well, exactly. It's acting as a huge hole, it's not acting in any way as an antenna.

To work as a slot antenna you'd have to have a low impedance feed right into the middle of each side of the hole, and for 144MHz the sides of your PC would need to be about 2.5 metres along each edge.

author: superkuh
text: You're talking about being right on resonance as if it won't help if it's off by 20% of the center frequency. But that's not true. Just like you can use a stumpy monopole whip for 144 Mhz even though it's 6 inches long, and it will help significantly (but behave like an omni capacitive reactance element), so will this not quite right slot antenna mode. There are many ways to excite and feed a slot antenna that do not depend on having the two excitation terminals on each side of the slot. Especially if you're doing it off frequency. Any conductor in the near field is going to couple via induction.

author: ErroneousBosh
text:
For receiving you can get away with nearly anything but for transmitting an aerial has to be quite close to resonant to be any good.

If you mean the little rubbery aerials on walkie-talkies, if you open one up you'll find it's around 50cm of wire coiled up. It's electrically still a quarter wavelength - there's no getting away from physics.

There really aren't.

author: ACCount39
text:
Yes, the mapping function is the thing you're missing.

When it comes to representational similarity analysis, we're trying to isolate the representations from the "coordinate systems" they sit in. If you take an image, and make a second image by rotating it 90 degrees and mirroring it, then, for the purposes of platonic representation hypothesis, they're the same image. Once you get past the "coordinate transform", the similarity between the first representation space and the 90-deg+mirror replica of it is total.

A mapping function between LE and BE can be constructed easily, and it's going to be lossless both ways. Which means that those two representations are fully compatible.

Now, INT16 and FP16? Those are far less compatible representations. There will be an overlap subspace where lossless conversion between the two is trivial, but this compatibility window will be relatively narrow.

text: The trick is to understand what is going on here: rather than a singular model trained for this exact job, this is performed by a awful hackjob of two models cut open and glued together at the seam. That glue layer is a single matrix, a fully connected layer, that is the only thing re-trained in the combined model. The rest of the coefficients are fixed. Naively, this shouldn't work - the internal representations of each model are unconstrained and should intuitively have completely different shapes. But this paper shows that this isn't quite the case: the difference between the latent spaces can be mostly expressed in a single matrix transform. And that allows that merged model to work at all.

The math can be misinterpreted, misapplied, or not fit reality. That's why high-assurance security mandated a combination of things:

1. English specification of the system and its goals

2. Formal, mathematical specification of the system and its goals

3. Mathematical proof the system met its goals

4. Code implementing that system with a proof, often informal, that the code embodied the informal and formal design.

5. Tests of all functionality to prove the design and code worked.

6. Independent analysis of the above to find flaws in them.

7. If the implementation has concurrency or parallelism, more errors can occur due to that. There were techniques to mitigate it.

Each step found problems in systems made by professionals. Mathematical work and coding both have a long history of errors in their on fields. Combining them increases the likelihood of error.

author: armcat
text:
I spent 10 years working with radio access networks (RAN), first in WCDMA (3G) then LTE (4G), then 5G. Our systems were also software defined radio (SDR), but, and this is crucial (and the paper points to this), the SDR as "malleable" as it is, is still highly dependent on the underlying hardware to achieve good performance.

Also, we spent huge amount of time making sure uplink performance is top-notch, as is the general stability and determinism, i.e. jitter and tail latency. In the paper they show that OAI is quite unstable, and they only achieve 5-49% of theoretical uplink capacity.

I keep getting clickbait youtube videos about how "NCM" obsoletes "LLMs" and "Nvidia memory chips" (yes, it's that bad).

This makes me wonder what these people think an "LLM" even is. The name itself implies that it is large and about language. It does not imply that an "LLM" is inherently autoregressive or that it has any particular architecture even though most LLMs are transformers. Anything can be a large language model as long as it is large and models language.

NCM is basically a hierarchical diffusion transformer where the further layers take one big token and then generate two smaller tokens. So it is more like an evaluation strategy. You could apply this to any model architecture.

I personally think the name NCM itself is terrible because it contains the word "next" which inherently implies an ordering and somehow we are supposed to think that "LLM" which contains no mention of ordering, is constrained to ordered token production.
